Every complement A satisfies the following for all large N, every squarefree Q ≤ N^{1−ε} and every residue r mod Q: #{a ≤ 2N : gcd(r−a, Q) = 1} ≥ (ε/2 − o(1))·(φ(Q)/Q)·log N. In particular, A mod Q is a c·(φ(Q)/Q)·log N-fold dominating set of ×_{p|Q} K_p.

(i) For Lebesgue-almost every α > 1 and every finite F, the set {⌊α^k⌋ : k ≥ 0} ∪ F is not a complement of the primes. This is new for 1 < α < e^{e^{−γ}} ≈ 1.753, where A(N) ≈ log N/log α exceeds e^γ·log N and Ruzsa does not apply. (ii) If A is random with P(a∈A) = C(log log a)/a and C < 1, then almost surely A is not a complement.

Three method limits. (i) If A has independent memberships and A(N) = o((log N)²) almost surely, then almost surely infinitely many n are not of the form p+a. Proof route: Kochen–Stone second Borel–Cantelli for the events {X_n = 0}, for the actual primes. (ii) Pure-CRT ceiling: h(P_Y) ≤ (1+o(1))·e^γ·θ(Y)·log Y. So no CRT-only argument proves more than (e^γ+o(1))·log N·log log N. (iii) Fractional ce
For every sequence of primes q_0<q_1<⋯ with q_{i+1} ≡ 1 (mod q_i), log q_k / k → ∞; equivalently q_k^{1/k} → ∞.

Assume the uniform Hardy–Littlewood upper bound for chain-shaped forms. That is, for each fixed c > 0, all large x, all K ≤ c log x/log log x, and all tuples with L_0 = n, L_t = m_t L_{t−1}+1, m_t ≥ 2, ∏m_t ≤ e^{K^2}: #{n ∈ (x,2x]: all L_t(n) prime} ≤ e^{o(K log K)} 𝔖(m) x/(log x)^{K+1}. Then every chain satisfies log p_k ≥ (1−o(1)) k log k, and in particular T1 holds. The proof must include the a

T1 follows from X_δ for some δ > 0 and c > 1/δ. X_δ: with K = ⌊c log x/log log x⌋ and Y = e^{AK}, #{(n,m): n ∈ (x,2x], ∏m ≤ Y, chain all prime} ≤ x(log x)^{−K−1} e^{(1−δ)K log K + O_A(K)}. Also prove that the fundamental lemma and Selberg's sieve give this exactly with δ = 0. X_δ is an averaged sieve statement, not equivalent to CORE.

There exist η > 0 and integers n_1<n_2<⋯ with the following properties: - n_{i+1} ≡ 1 (mod n_i); - n_j ≢ 0 (mod n_i) for i < j; - every prime factor of n_i exceeds η log n_i; - log n_k = (log 2 + o(1)) k. Hence no argument using only divisibility by primes ≤ η log p can prove liminf p_k^{1/k} > 2. Construction: A1 run pattern; Q*(r) | n+1 at run starts; bridges chosen by CRT. The cost of steering
For every chain, limsup m_i = ∞. Equivalently, no finite S has m_i ∈ S for all large i.
Every chain has m_i ≥ 18 for infinitely many i. That is, S = {2,4,…,16} in full is excluded, including {8,14} and all 4- to 8-subsets.
Under GRH, every chain has log p_k ≥ k log 2 + k^{α−o(1)} for some explicit α > 0. Ideally α = log2/log(2+log2/A) ≈ 0.514, matching the A1 construction.
For every finite S ⊂ 2ℤ_{>0}, the locally admissible shift X_S = ∩_q X_q has topological entropy 0. Here X_q is the set of multiplier words admitting a residue orbit mod q that avoids 0.
In F_2[t], for every D there is no chain of irreducibles P_{i+1} = M_i P_i + 1 with deg M_i ≤ D for all large i.

In Granville's random-prime model (n is "prime" with probability ∏_{q≤y}(1−1/q)^{−1}/log n if n is y-rough, y = log n): - almost surely every chain has log p_k ≥ (1−o(1)) k log k; - some chain has log p_k ≤ (1+o(1)) k log k.
For every strictly increasing n with n_k/k→∞, every a_k ≠ 0 and every entire f = Σa_k z^{n_k}, and every w ∈ ℂ, the set f^{-1}(w) is infinite.

Finite lower order λ gives r_j → ∞ with log M(8r_j) ≤ K·log M(r_j/2), K = 16^{λ+1}. 3. Let E = {θ : Re g(r_j e^{iθ}) < 0}. Since ∫u⁻ = 2πT(r,e^g) + O(1), Edrei–Fuchs gives |E|·log(e/|E|) ≥ c/K. 4. If f has finite hyper-order (log log log M(r) = O(log r)) and n_k/(k·log k·log log k) → ∞, then f takes every value infinitely often. This covers the non-Fejér case n_k = k log k loglog k logloglog k.
For f of finite hyper-order, the gap condition (n_{k+1}−n_k)/log n_k → ∞ suffices. This removes the log log loss in T3, and the condition is implied by n_k/(k log k) → ∞ with locally regular gaps.

Any counterexample f, with exceptional value a, has all of the following: - (i) infinite lower order; - (ii) Σ1/n_k = ∞; - (iii) for all large r outside a set of finite logarithmic measure, N(C·ν(r))·log log M(r) ≥ c·log M(r); - (iv) a tract on which log|f−a| ≤ −c·T(|z|,f) holds on a set of angular measure ≥ (log M)^{-2}.

Assuming Erdős Problem #516 (the Pólya-type conjecture: Fabry gaps imply limsup log m(r)/log M(r) = 1), the full statement holds. In fact the weak form limsup m(r) = ∞, assumed only for f of infinite lower order, already suffices.

There is an entire f with Fabry gaps, of infinite lower order, such that log m(r) ≤ (1−c)·log M(r) for all r outside a set of finite logarithmic measure. In other words, Fuchs's theorem fails beyond finite order.
Let F(s) = Σ a_k e^{λ_k s} be an entire Dirichlet series with real λ_k ↑ ∞, λ_k/k → ∞, infinitely many a_k ≠ 0, and finite Ritt order. Then F takes every value infinitely often.

Fabry gaps together with finite lower order give δ(a,f) = 0 for every finite a. Proof sketch: suppose δ(a,f) > 0. Edrei–Fuchs gives a set E′ of measure ≥ c on which |f−a| ≤ e^{−δT/4} along the radii r_j of T2. Truncating f−a at X ≈ log M(2r_j) makes the tail ≤ e^{−δT/4}. Nazarov's lemma then gives log M(r_j) = o(log M(r_j)), a contradiction.

Let X be the statement "every Fabry-gap entire function of infinite lower order is unbounded on every curve to ∞". Then T2 + X ⇒ CORE. Proof: 1. Suppose f has finitely many a-points, so f−a = P·e^g. 2. Components of {|f−a| < ε} that avoid the zeros are unbounded, by the minimum principle. 3. Nesting such components as ε → 0 gives a path on which f → a, so f is bounded on that path. 4. This contrad
There exist a type V and G : SimpleGraph V with G.chromaticCardinal = ℵ₁ such that for every countable s ⊆ V, G.induce s is not infinitely connected.
Under ◇, there is a graph G on ω₁ with χ(G)=ℵ₁ (K_{ℵ₀,ℵ₀}-free, Hajnal–Máté condition) such that no countable induced subgraph is infinitely connected.
Under Martin's Maximum (MM), every graph with χ(G)=ℵ₁, of any cardinality, contains a countable infinitely connected induced subgraph.

In ZFC, there is a ladder-system graph on ω₁ with no countable infinitely connected subgraph. Each limit δ is joined exactly to a ladder L_δ ⊆ δ of successor ordinals, so col(G)=ℵ₁ automatically by Fodor/elementarity; χ(G)=2.
(ZFC) Every graph with χ(G) ≥ ℵ₂ contains a countable infinitely connected subgraph. Fallback: every graph with col(G) ≥ ℵ₂ contains K_{ℵ₀,ℵ₀}.

Every uncountably chromatic ladder graph on a non-special tree (Soukup's ZFC construction) contains a countable infinitely connected subgraph. Likewise every Erdős–Hajnal–Shelah type graph on [κ]^n with χ>ℵ₀ contains K_{ℵ₀,ℵ₀}.

If any counterexample exists, then there is one G with all of the following properties: - G is K_{ℵ₀,ℵ₀}-free; - G contains an infinite bipartite half-graph; - col(G) ≤ 2^{ℵ₀}; - every maximal ℵ₀-block Y has G[Y] ω-degenerate, hence χ(G[Y]) ≤ ℵ₀. Conversely, any K_{ℵ₀,ℵ₀}-free G with χ=ℵ₁ and all blocks ω-degenerate is a counterexample.
Every analytic graph on a Polish space with uncountable (abstract) chromatic number contains K_{ℵ₀,ℵ₀}, hence a countable infinitely connected subgraph.

T2 follows from Lemma X. There is a property P of graphs on countable ordinals with four features: - (i) P is closed under increasing ω-unions; - (ii) P implies no infinitely connected subgraph; - (iii) P implies K_{ℵ₀,ℵ₀}-freeness; - (iv) for every H on δ with P and every countable family of sets cofinal in δ, there is a ladder L ⊆ δ meeting each set such that H+δ (joined to L) has P. Under PFA (so 𝔠 = ℵ₂), every graph of size ℵ₂ with χ=ℵ₁ contains a countable infinitely connected subgraph.
For every M ∈ ℕ there is n₀ with h(n) ≥ M for all n ≥ n₀, i.e. h(n) → ⊤ in ℕ∞ (with non-strict 1-separation).
Determine D(9) exactly and all 9-point minimisers up to congruence; in particular decide whether h(9)=1.
There exists n with h(n) ≥ 2 (expected: some n with h(n)=⊤, via a certified minimiser containing a rattler or a non-diametral hull point).

There are absolute constants C, C′ such that every minimiser A for n points satisfies: - conv(A) has minimal width ≥ D(n) − C; - conv(A) lies within Hausdorff distance C′n^{1/4} of a disk of diameter D(n).

Let X(n) be the statement "some minimiser for n points is not locally jammed": some point of A ∩ ∂conv(A) is not a diameter endpoint, or some point of A ∖ ∂conv(A) has all its distance-1 neighbours in a closed half-plane. Then X(n) ⇒ h(n) = ⊤. Hence "X(n) for all large n" ⇒ CORE. Formalise this in Lean against the given definitions.

Let Λ be the triangular (Eisenstein) lattice with unit spacing, and h_Λ(n) the number of congruence classes of n-subsets of Λ of minimal diameter. Decide whether h_Λ(n) → ∞: either prove h_Λ(n) ≥ 2 for all n ≥ n₀, or exhibit infinitely many n with h_Λ(n) = 1.

Assume the boundary-crystallization hypothesis (a finite-crystallization statement of Heitmann–Radin type; no standard named conjecture covers this problem): for all large n some minimiser A has A ∩ ∂conv(A) contained in a congruent copy of the triangular lattice. Then h(n) = ⊤ for all large n. Proof plan: - Diameters pairwise cross, so their directions are distinct. - Lattice vectors of length D
D(n) < D(n+1) for all n ≥ 3; hence the deletion method yields no minimisers for any n ≥ 3.
h(n) = ⊤ for infinitely many n, and ideally for a set of n of density 1.
Improve the second-order term: show D(n) ≤ c√n − δ, or D(n) ≥ c√n − √3/2 + δ, for some δ > 0 and all large n (c = (2√3/π)^{1/2}).

There exist complementary A, B ⊆ ℕ and bijections f: ℕ → A, g: ℕ → B such that neither (f(n))_n nor (g(n))_n has indices i < j < k whose values form a nonconstant arithmetic progression (exactly the Lean statement erdos_197).

For s_k = k² (or any s_k → ∞ with s_k = o(2^k) and 2s_k − s_{k+1} → ∞), the set A'_s = ⋃_{k even}(2^k + s_k, 2^{k+1}] is permutable. Consequently some permutable set has d_lower + d_upper = 1 (lower 1/3, upper 2/3), attaining the knife-edge supremum.

Let T_k = 2^k + s_k with s_k → ∞, s_{k+1} < 2s_k and 2s_k − s_{k+1} → ∞ (e.g. s_k = k²). Both classes are permutable: - A_s = ⋃_{k even}(T_k, T_{k+1}]; - B_s = ⋃_{k odd}(T_k, T_{k+1}] ∪ [0, T_0]. Hence YES.

If A ⊆ ℕ is permutable and contains an interval of 16 consecutive integers, then A contains (M, 2M] for only finitely many M. Corollary: in any witness partition only finitely many doubling intervals (M, 2M] are monochromatic.
For all c ≥ 1, E ≥ 0 and every integer sequence T_k with |T_k − c·2^k| ≤ E, the class ⋃_{k even}(T_k, T_{k+1}] is not permutable. So no bounded perturbation of the dyadic partition is a witness.

- Proved implication: for 2-automatic A ⊆ ℕ and a 2-automatic relation ≺, "≺ is a linear order of type ω on A with no monotone 3-AP" is a sentence of ⟨ℕ, +, V₂⟩, hence decidable. ("Type ω" is expressible as ∀y ∃N ∀x (x ≺ y → x < N).) So YES follows from X: some 2-automatic colouring has 2-automatic good orders on both classes. - Target: decide X for the automatic T3 candidate with twisted bit-reve

Each state records, for the top-spill and bottom-spill windows of a block, the ranks modulo the twisted-order pattern. - Every block k of A_s and of B_s admits an AP-free ordering f
Let A_p contain each n independently with probability p_n. - If p_n ≡ p ∈ (0, 1), A_p is almost surely not permutable. - If p_n → 0, A_p is almost surely permutable.
In any witness (A, B), the octave densities a_t = |A ∩ (2^t, 2^{t+1}]|/2^t satisfy a_t(1 − a_t) → 0 and a_t + a_{t+1} → 1 (macroscopic dyadic rigidity).
No colouring of the form c(n) = Φ(⌊log₂ n⌋ mod L, n mod q), for any L, q and Φ, is a witness.

Let N ≥ 2, let m₀ = m₀(N) be the least m with Σ_{n=N}^{N+m−1} 1/n ≥ 1, and put M = N + m₀ − 2, so that Σ_N^M 1/n < 1 ≤ Σ_N^{M+1} 1/n. Assume hypothesis H(N): there are ≥ 8 primes in (2(M+1)/3, 5M/6], 2(M+1)/3 ≥ max(N,5), and M+1 ≥ 14. Then:
k(N) = m₀(N) ⟺ R_N := 1 − Σ_{n=N}^{M} 1/n = 1/b for some integer b.
In that case b > M+1, and the unique S with |S| = m₀ and Σ_S 1/n = 1 is [N,M] ∪ {b}. Otherwise k(N) ≥ m₀(N)+1. H(N) holds for every N ≥ 112 (s3.py checks 112 ≤ N ≤ 10^6, and Dusart's bounds cover the rest; see AUDIT).

targets.statement: k(N) − (e−1)N → ∞ as N → ∞ (the Lean statement erdos_295).

k(N) ≤ (e−1)N + O(log N). Proof plan: - Let M be maximal with Σ_{n=N}^{M} 1/n < 1. Then M − N + 1 = (e−1)N + O(1). - The remainder ρ = a/b has b | lcm(N..M), so log log b ≤ log N + O(1). - [025] writes ρ as O(log log b) distinct unit fractions. - Each of them is ≤ ρ ≤ 1/(M+1), so all are new and distinct from the interval.

Strengthen the KNOWN structure lemma as follows. If |S| ≤ (e−1)N + C, then all but o(π(eN)) primes p ∈ [N^{1/2+ε},(1−δ)eN] divide an element of S above (1+δ)eN. Consequently ∏_{far} n ≥ exp((e − O(δ) − o(1))N). For r = 1 the far element b satisfies b | lcm(S'), b ≡ −p/H_p (mod p²), and b ≥ lcm(S')·e^{−O(δN)}.

For each C there is N₀(C) such that for N ≥ N₀ no representation 1 = Σ_S 1/n with S ⊂ [N,∞) and |S| ≤ (e−1)N + C has exactly one element exceeding 3N. That is, the case r = 1: the numerator of 1 − Σ_{S'} 1/n is never 1 for near-interval S' ⊂ [N,3N].
Let k_X(N) be k(N) with all denominators ≤ X. For N² ≤ X ≤ exp(N/log N): k_X(N) − (e−1)N = Θ(N/log X).

Assume Hypothesis H, defined as follows. For every fixed r, and every rational ρ = a/D whose reduced denominator is divisible by at least half the primes of [N,2N], if ρ is a sum of r distinct unit fractions then a ≥ D·exp(−o(N)). Then CORE holds. No standard named conjecture (GRH, abc, Hypothesis H of Schinzel) is known to us to imply CORE. H is a non-standard, "typical-numerator Erdős–Graham" ty
For every R, the set {N : k(N) ≤ (e−1)N + R} has natural density 0.
For all large N and any θ > 1/2, there are S' (near-interval) and at most 3 integers b_j > eN such that Σ_{S'} 1/n + Σ_j 1/b_j has reduced denominator free of primes > N^θ.

Let X ⊂ ℝ² be valid, Γ a circle, A = X ∩ Γ with a = |A| ≥ 3, and suppose X ⊄ Γ. Then D(X) ≥ 3a/4 − 1.
Equivalently: if X is valid, not concyclic, then every circle contains at most (4/3)(D(X)+1) points of X. In particular, if
D(X) ≤ (1+δ)n/2 and X is not concyclic, every circle holds ≤ (2/3)(1+δ)n + 4/3 points.

Let X be valid and in strictly convex position, with hull order v_0,…,v_{n−1}. Let d_1 > d_2 > … be its distances, and def_j = Σ_x (2 − deg_{d_j}(x)), so that Σ_j def_j = nΔ. Then every chord v_a v_b with |v_a v_b| = d_j has cyclic order min(|a−b|, n−|a−b|) ≥ (n−1)/2 − 4(j−1) − def_j/4. In particular, if Δ = 0, every d_j-chord has order ≥ k − 4(j−1) with k = (n−1)/2. If Δ ≤ 1, X is automatically convex by C2.

Let X ⊂ ℝ² be finite and valid (no circle centred at a point of X contains ≥3 other points of X). Let C be a circle, Y = X ∩ C, m = |Y| ≥ 1. If D(X) < 3m/4 − 1, then X ⊂ C and X lies in the vertex set of a regular h-gon inscribed in C with h = |A−A| ≤ 2D(X)+1 (A = angle set of X).
Corollary: X valid, not concyclic ⇒ every circle contains ≤ (4/3)(D(X)+1) points of X.

targets.statement: ∀ c > 0, ∃ᶠ n in atTop, ∃ X : Finset ℝ², #X = n ∧ IsValid X ∧ distinctDistances X < (1+c)n/2. Explicitly, for every n ≥ 3 the vertex set of the regular n-gon is valid and determines exactly ⌊n/2⌋ nonzero distances.
If n = 2k+1 ≥ 5, X is valid and D(X) = k, then X is the vertex set of a regular n-gon.
There is a c > 0 such that every convex-position valid X with no four concyclic points has D(X) ≥ (1+c)n/2. More strongly, convex valid X with D ≤ (1+δ)n/2 has ≥ (1−ε)n points concyclic.
Let X be valid and contained in the union of two circles (or a circle and a line), with each part of size ≥ εn. Then D(X) ≥ (1+c(ε))n/2.
Every valid X with no four concyclic points has D(X) ≥ n/2 + f(n) for some f(n) → ∞, for instance f(n) = c·log n.
CORE (S). For every ε > 0 there is a δ > 0 such that every valid X with D ≤ (1+δ)n/2 has ≥ (1−ε)n concyclic points.

Let I(X) be the number of apex-labelled isosceles triangles (x; {y,z}) with |xy| = |xz|. For valid X, D(X) ≥ n − 1 − I(X)/n. Hence the general-position version of #655 follows from the claim: (R) Every valid X with no 3 collinear and no 4 concyclic satisfies I(X) ≤ (1/2 − η)n², i.e. the average number of apexes per pair is ≤ 1 − 2η. Proof of the implication: point x sees n − 1 − s₂(x) distances, w
Assume the linear form of Erdős #98: h(n) ≥ (1/2 + η)n for sets with no 3 collinear and no 4 concyclic. Then every valid X with no 4 concyclic (collinear triples allowed) has D(X) ≥ (1/2 + η′)n.

Let f_k(n) be the minimum of D(X) over n-point sets X in which every circle centred at a point of X contains ≤ k other points. Then f_3(n) ≥ (1/2 − o(1))n, or else an explicit family achieves f_3(n) ≤ (1/2 − δ)n.
Let X = A ∪ B be valid, where A is concyclic, B is disjoint from the circle, and 1 ≤ |B| ≤ K. Then D(X) ≥ (1+c)n/2 for n ≥ n₀(K). For K = 1, D(X) ≥ n − O(1) when A is a regular polygon.

validated.statement: Assume GRH. For n ≥ n0, λ(n) ≤ max(P°(n), 27 (log n)²). Hence c(n) ≤ (2 max(P°(n), 27 log² n))^n. For odd n this gives c(n) ≤ exp((2+o(1)) n log log n), and log c(n) ≤ n log max(P°(n), log² n) + O(n) for all n.

(a) For every odd n ≥ 253, gcd{aⁿ − 1 : 2 ≤ a ≤ L}=1 where L = ⌊n/4⌋+1.
(b) Hence every k ≥ 1 + (2ⁿ−2)(Lⁿ−1) is admissible, and the cutoff c(n) (which exists and is unique) satisfies c(n) < (2L)ⁿ ≤ (n/2+2)ⁿ.
(c) TSLowerBound is false: for all A, B > 0 and all N, there are an odd n ≥ N and a c with IsCutoff n c and B·c < A·nⁿ.

Let n ≥ 1 and L ≥ 2 with L ≥ P(n) (largest prime p with p−1 | n) and Ψ(L², L) > n, where Ψ(x, y) = #{1 ≤ m ≤ x : every prime factor of m is ≤ y}. Then gcd{aⁿ−1 : 2 ≤ a ≤ L} = 1.
Hence λ(n) ≤ max(P(n), L*(n)) with L*(n) := min{L ≥ 2 : Ψ(L², L) > n}, and c(n) < (2·max(P(n), L*(n)))ⁿ.
Asymptotically L*(n) = (1+o(1))·√(n/(1−log 2)) ≈ 1.805√n. So for odd n (P(n) = 2):
- c(n) ≤ (3.611+o(1))ⁿ·n^{n/2};
- λ(n) ≤ (1.805+o(1))√n.

targets.statement: ¬TSLowerBound. Equivalently, for all A, B > 0 and every N there are n ≥ N and c with IsCutoff n c and B·c < A·nⁿ. Quantitatively, for all odd n ≥ n₀, c(n) ≤ 1 + (2^n − 2)·Σ_{a=3}^{⌈0.45n⌉+1}(a^n − 1). Hence c(n)/nⁿ → 0 along odd n.
For all n, c(n) ≤ e^{o(n)}·(P(n)^n + n^{0.7n}). Here P(n) is the largest prime with p − 1 | n, and P(n) ≤ n/2 + 1 when n+1 is composite. In particular, c(n) = o(nⁿ) unless n+1 is prime.
- (a) Under GRH, c(n) ≤ (log n)^{O(n)} for odd n. - (b) Under Ailon–Rudnick for (2, 3), c(n) < 6^n for infinitely many n.

For each prime p with p − 1 | n, let K_p(n) be the minimal number of cubes in a tiling having a side with v_p ≠ 0. Then c(n) ≥ K_p(n) − p + 1. More generally, the same holds for any p | 2^n − 1, with "side outside H_p" in place of "v_p ≠ 0".
If n+1 is prime, then c(n) ≥ n^{(1−o(1))n}. The strong form is c(n) ≥ εnⁿ.
For even n, c(n) ≥ (2+δ)^n. Route: every tiling with a side of nonzero 3-adic valuation has ≥ (2+δ)^n cubes, then apply T6.
Every tiling with fewer than 3^n − 2^n + 1 cubes is dyadic, i.e. all sides are 2^{−j}. Consequently k ≡ 1 mod (2^n − 1) for such tilings, and c(n) ≥ 3^n − 2^{n+1} + 3.
For the split semigroup ⟨a^n − 1 : a ≥ 2⟩ with Frobenius number F_n, prove log F_n = n·log λ*(n) + O(n). Here λ*(n) = max over primes p | 2^n − 1 of the least a with p ∤ a^n − 1.

Let 0 < s < √2, φ_s = 2 arcsin(s/2) (< π/2), κ_s = 2 s √(φ_s / sin φ_s). Let A be a 1-separated n-set with
diam A = D(n), P = conv A. If p, q ∈ A ∩ ∂P with |pq| ≤ s, then the line ℓ = pq supports P (so [p,q] ⊂ ∂P, i.e. p,q on one
edge of P), provided
  (√3/2)·( (π/(2√3))(D − 2/√3)² − 1 − πD/2 ) > (φ_s/2) D² + κ_s D     (*)
holds at D = D(n). (*) holds for all D > D*(s); D*(1) ≈ 20.50, D*(1.2) ≈ 41.9, D*(1.4) ≈ 666. Since
n ≤ (π/(2√3))D(n)² + πD(n)/2 + 1, (*) holds for all n ≥ n0(s): n0(1)=415, n0(1.2)≈1662, n0(1.4)≈4·10^5.

Let L≥1 and M≥1 be integers, k≥2, and c: ℤ/M→{1..k}. Put P(n)=⌊L·log₂ n⌋ (n≥1), χ(n)=c(P(n) mod M),

colouring χ'(n)=c'(P'(n) mod 8) is a 2-automatic 3-colouring with no witness.

(a) ψ has no constant [n,n+2] with n≥2, so it has bounded runs (R=4). ψ(2n)=ψ(n) for every odd n, and ψ(2n)≠ψ(n) for every even n≥2.
(b) If u∈ℕ*, t∈ℤ and ψ̃(2u+t)=ψ̃(u+u+t), then α(u):=u-lim n∈ℤ₂ is not in ℚ.
(c) Finitary form: if B⊆ℕ is infinite, t∈ℤ and ψ is constant on B+B+t, then every 2-adic accumulation point of B is irrational.
COROLLARY: Let S⊆ℚ∩ℤ₂. No argument whose witnesses u always have α(u)∈S proves L6 or bounded-run Owings. With C4, any adequate S must meet E_q for every odd q≥3 AND contain 2-adic irrationals.

(a) Let x∈(1/2,1) be irrational, with binary digits x=Σ_{i≥1} t_i 2^{-i}, and θ=1/x. Put ψ_θ(n)=(⌊log₂(θn)⌋+n) mod 2. (b) Lacunary defects. Let Δ⊆ℕ_{≥2}, δ(n)=|Δ∩[1,n]|, and ψ(n)=(n+δ(n)) mod 2. Suppose infinitely many d∈Δ have no element of Δ in (d,2d−2] ("good" d). Then ψ is constant on B+B for an infinite B.

For an odd q≥3 put ψ_q(n)=(⌊log₂(qn)⌋+n) mod 2 for n≥1, and set ψ_q(0) arbitrarily. For u∈ℕ* let α(u)∈ℤ₂ be the 2-adic limit u-lim n. Let E_q={e/q : e∈ℤ, q∤e}⊂ℤ₂. Then:
(a) ψ_q has no constant [n,n+2] with n≥2, so it has bounded runs. ψ_q(2n)=ψ_q(n) for every odd n.
(b) For every u∈ℕ* with α(u)∉E_q and every t∈ℤ: ψ̃_q(2u+t)≠ψ̃_q(u+u+t). So the only ultrafilters that can witness non-shift-freeness of ψ_q have α(u)∈E_q.
(c) Witnesses do exist: ψ_q≡0 on B+B for B={(2^K−1)/q : K≡0 mod 2·ord_q(2)}. Here α=−1/q∈E_q.
COROLLARY (obstruction): Let S⊆ℤ₂ be any set with S∩E_q=∅ for some odd q≥3. Then no argument whose witnesses u always satisfy α(u)∈S can prove L6, or Owings for bounded-run 2-colourings. Examples of such S:
- S=ℤ (all of ℤ+H, which includes IP/idempotent methods and all translates x+p);
- S=ℤ₂∖ℚ (only 2-adically irrational ultrafilters);
- S=ℤ[1/M]∩ℤ₂ for any fixed odd M (take a prime q∤M).
Finitary form: if B is infinite, t∈ℤ, and ψ_q is constant on B+B+t, then every 2-adic accumulation point of B lies in E_q. Proof: each accumulation point is α(u) for some nonprincipal u∋B, and such a u has ψ̃_q(2u+t)=ψ̃_q(u+u+t), because B+B+t∈u+u+t and 2B+t∈2u+t.
So a proof must produce, for EVERY odd prime q, witnesses at 2-adically rational points whose denominator is exactly q. These cannot be confined to ℤ, nor to the irrationals, nor to any fixed set of denominators.
